title: Bucktown camps and the lake steamboats
summary: Bucktown was summer camps with weekend dances; steamers like the Susquehanna and Mandeville ran to Mandeville with mostly black bands, and a wooden leg of Bob Aguilera turned up in the union attic.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: What was going on in Bucktown in those days?

Bucktown was camps. They'd have camps and really, everything happened on like say weekends in the summertime. Where people would go, they'd rent a camp and like instead of going to Florida for a week or two weeks like they do now, they'd rent a camp at Bucktown. You didn't have to travel to go there and it was the same effect. You could go swimming in the lake and it was close enough that if a man was still, even if it was working, he could get to work. And then the family could go out there and spend a week or so. Was there any music happening out there? On weekends they used to have like dances. And then you used to have right there on the lake there, right there at the New Basin Canal, they had the steamer, steamboats, I'll call them not steam ships, they're steamboats. They used to go over to Mandeville, the Susquehanna, and I can't remember all the names of the... You knew those things. Well, I've heard about them, I've seen pictures of them. Susquehanna.
I've known people, there's somebody back in town who used to work on the Susquehanna.

Yeah, and in fact, the funny thing about it, that lake, Partchertrain, is a very, very shallow lake. And that's why when it storms out there, it's so bad because, I mean, it's shallow and the waves can, there's no place for them to go. And I remember many times we'd get out there on that Susquehanna, or the Mandeville, there was a mother boat by the name of the Mandeville, that you would be dancing and you'd be dancing along and you'd hit the bottom of the lake, the boat was hitting the bottom of the lake like that. You'd bounce it like that.
Were you playing on those boats?

No, they usually used colored bands. They had some white bands on it. I can't remember the names, I don't know. I can reach you, I can go get my book and I can tell you right now, with all the different bands, Happy Shilling's band, George Shilling, his father. Yeah. And there was another one, Bob Aguilera used to play on those bands, the pillar with one leg. I told you when I did the, I was in charge of redoing the Musicians Union over when we renewed it, when we rejuvenated it. We went up in the attic and found one of Bob Aguilera's wooden legs.
Give it to the Jazz Museum.
